title: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Cellular automata that produce only uniform or repetitive patterns (class 1 and class 2) can never be universal, because they transmit information only over limited distances and so support only processes involving a limited number of cells.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: In a sense the fundamental reason for this—as we discussed on page 252—is that such class 1 and class 2 cellular automata never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “The Threshold of Universality in Cellular Automata” (from p. 694), p. 694. Scope: class 1 and class 2 cellular automata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-19: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Under the bounded-information interpretation stated in the claim, a clean impossibility proof is available. Ambiguity in assigning all cellular automata to phenomenological classes slightly weakens full-scope certainty.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Give rigorous dynamical definitions of class 1 and class 2 with bounded information propagation, then prove that their bounded communication or eventual periodicity cannot implement arbitrarily large universal computations.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Wolfram classes are phenomenological rather than uniquely formal.

Some formal definitions of class 2 may not imply a uniform propagation bound.

fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: If the class is defined by ultimately uniform or repetitive behavior for every input, non-universality is a theorem: only finitely much information about the input survives, or the surviving information is periodic. That argument can be checked on the elementary examples by computing periods and dependence cones. The book's phrase about limited distance is slightly too narrow for shifting class-2 rules, but those rules still fail universality for the same periodicity reason.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Formalize class 1 and class 2 as evolution that, for every initial condition, becomes uniform or periodic with a bound depending only on the rule. Prove that such a system has a finite effective memory and cannot emulate a Turing machine. A universality construction inside that class would refute the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: Some rules usually called class 2 carry signals arbitrarily far, so non-universality then rests on the form of the reachable configurations rather than on a strict distance bound.

fields.label: Dimension scores

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Every elementary cellular automaton that settles into a uniform or short-period state from random initial conditions (operational class 1 or 2) transmits a single-cell perturbation of that settled state only over a bounded distance, whereas rules that do not settle spread perturbations without bound.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py runs all 256 rules: 10 seeded random initial conditions on an 800-cell ring, 1000 steps, period detection up to 64 steps, then a single-cell flip of the settled configuration and 400 further steps for both copies; damage width = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1. Operational class 1/2 = >= 9/10 trials settled; bounded = max width <= 20; spreading = median width >= 100. The Wikipedia page is fetched for its checksum and the example rules per class are checked against the operational classification. Per-rule values in derived/rules.csv (including a post-hoc width at step 200), fetch record in derived/wikipedia.json; runtime about 50 s.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules. For each rule, 10 trials: ring of N = 800 cells, random initial condition with density 1/2 (numpy default_rng seed 20261033), evolve 1000 steps to configuration C; the trial is 'settled' if C recurs within the next 64 steps (temporal period <= 64, which includes uniform and shifted-periodic states). A rule is 'operational class 1/2' if >= 9 of 10 trials settle. In every settled trial, flip one cell of C (the cell at index 400) and evolve both copies 400 further steps on the ring (N = 800 > 2 x 400, so the damage cannot wrap); record the damage width w = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1 (0 if none). A rule is 'bounded' if w <= 20 in all of its settled trials, 'spreading' if the median w over settled trials >= 100 (linear growth), otherwise 'intermediate'. The claim PASSES if 100% of operational class 1/2 rules are 'bounded'. Validation (reported, not decisive): the rules Wikipedia cites as Wolfram's class 1 and 2 examples (0, 32, 160, 232; 4, 108, 218, 250) must be operational class 1/2 and the class 3 and 4 examples (22, 30, 126, 150, 182; 110, 54) must not be; and the fraction of non-settled rules that are 'spreading' is reported.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if any operational class 1/2 rule is 'spreading' (a settled rule that nevertheless transmits a perturbation over a linearly growing region). If some class 1/2 rules are 'intermediate' but none 'spreading', the verdict is 'mixed'. If the Wikipedia example rules are misclassified by the operational definition, that is reported as a caveat on the mapping to Wolfram's phenomenological classes but does not change the verdict.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of operational class 1/2 rules whose settled-state perturbation stays bounded (width <= 20 after 400 steps)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: 96 operational class 1/2 rules; 94 bounded, 2 intermediate, 0 spreading

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The claim has a conclusion (class 1 and 2 automata cannot be universal) and a stated mechanism ('never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances'). Non-universality is a statement about all possible encodings and is not testable by finite computation; the test addresses the mechanism, which is the premise of Wolfram's argument: perturbations of class 1/2 states stay localized. Wolfram's classes are phenomenological, so they are operationalised here as 'settles into a temporal cycle of period <= 64 on an 800-cell ring within 1000 steps from random initial conditions'; the damage width (not displacement) is used so that shifting class-2 rules, whose perturbation moves but does not grow, count as bounded, as the assessors noted. Perturbations are applied to the settled state because the claim concerns the asymptotic behaviour, not transients.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value:
256 elementary cellular automata, settled states and single-cell perturbations (generated by analysis.py)

Wikipedia, 'Elementary cellular automaton' (example rules for Wolfram's four classes)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Pre-registered decision: 0 of 96 operational class 1/2 rules is 'spreading', so the claim is not refuted, but 2 rules (37 and 62) are 'intermediate' (max damage width 24 and 27 in one trial each, medians 2.0 and 1.5), so the pre-registered rule gives 'mixed' rather than 'supports'. The 20-cell threshold was set before the run; with a 30-cell threshold every class 1/2 rule would be bounded.

Post-hoc inspection shows the two intermediate cases are static, not growing: the damage width at step 200 equals the width at step 400 (rule 37: 24:24, 21:21; rule 62: 28:27). The six class 1/2 trials whose width is larger at step 400 than at step 200 are period-2 oscillations between widths 1 and 2 in rule 62. Substantively the mechanism Wolfram states (perturbations of class 1/2 states stay localised) holds for all 96 rules; the 'mixed' verdict reflects a conservative threshold rather than a counterexample.

All 14 Wikipedia example rules are classified as expected by the operational definition (class 1 and 2 examples settle in 10/10 trials with max width <= 4; class 3 and 4 examples never settle), so the operational class maps onto Wolfram's phenomenological classes for these rules. 160 rules are not operational class 1/2; 7 of them settle in some trials, and in 5 of those (rules 14, 57, 99, 113, 143) the perturbation of the settled state spreads across the whole ring, consistent with the converse.

The test addresses the stated mechanism (bounded information transmission), not the conclusion (impossibility of universality), which concerns all encodings and is not finitely testable. Results depend on the finite ring (800 cells), horizon (1000 + 400 steps), the single-flip perturbation and one random seed; shifting class 2 rules are counted as bounded by using width rather than displacement.
